name: Theona
description:
Theona

Key Demographics: Humans

Capital City: Inis na gCúig

Quick Reference

Tagline: The Green Host rides for those who count to nine. Viterra counts to nine. The Everflame burns the ninth.

Abbess Caelia of Whiterick (Everflame):

“The Viterran sheriffs count heads for tax. The Moot-keepers count steps for safety. I count souls for salvation. Nine is a sin. Eight is a compromise. Only the Flame is whole.”

Matron of Wells (Theona):

“The wells here hold more than water—they hold the dreams and the breath of generations. The Viterran sheriffs call it superstition. The Abbess calls it heresy. The Green Host calls it trespass.”

Theme & Atmosphere

The isles of Theona rise green and jagged from the Dolmis, their basalt cliffs wrapped in mists and moorland song. Nominally a duchy sworn to Viterra, in truth the Three Greens heed no crown but their own moots, no law but their taboos. The greatest of these is the silence of Nine: no bell tolls a ninth, no bridge counts that span, no oath dares its syllable. It is said that those who break the ban invite the Green Host—the Aos S', the elder folk who were here before the first Viterran longship.

The Viterran crown claims the isles by right of conquest and papal bull. Its sheriffs impose common law, its bishops raise stone steeples. But the Church of the Everflame watches from Whiterick Abbey. The Abbess schemes to preserve power by pitting Viterra, the native factions, and raiders against each other, seeking to purge the “pagan” taboos and impose imperial orthodoxy. To break a taboo is to invite not only the fae but the inquisitor. The sheriff leaves a noose. The Host leaves a hollow in the mist where your name used to be. The Abbess leaves a brand that burns until confession.

What you notice first: The smell of wet peat and salt. The silence that follows every eighth bell-ring. The hawthorn and blackthorn trees at every crossroads—the fairy thorns that no local will touch, and that Viterran surveyors learn to skirt after the first one disappears.

The one rule that kills newcomers: Never pour the ninth cup at a feast. Never speak the ninth name in a bargain. Never step where a step is missing. The Green Host rides for those who complete what should remain incomplete. The Viterran sheriff will hang you for the same offense—but the Host takes your name, not your neck. The Everflame Inquisitor will burn you for the silence itself.

The Gray Liturgy: A Syncretic Faith of Theona

Deep in the mist-shrouded valleys and along the tide-cut stairs of Theona, a different faith endures—one that does not flee the Ninth but approaches it with ritual, witness, and the patient weight of carried secrets. The Gray Liturgy is not a foreign import. It is the old faith that was nearly erased, pushed to the fens, the barrows, the places where the ninth step is already half-taken. Its practitioners are not priests. They are keeners (who sing the dead across), well-walkers (who tend the threshold-wells), and taboo-breakers (who have taken the ninth step and returned—changed, but alive).

Where Theona's folk practice avoids the Ninth, the Gray Liturgy engages it—ritually, carefully, with witnesses and salt and the Shepherd's lantern. They are not heretics. They are the ones who remember what the Ninth actually is: not a demon, not a curse, but a door that was left unlocked. The Gray Liturgy carries the key.

The Saints of the Threshold (Syncretic Patrons)

The Gray Liturgy teaches that before the True Light came to 'Eire, there were the Naomh na Tairs'—the Saints of the Threshold. They were not gods. They were the first to cross from death to life and return. They guide the living, carry the dead, and keep the doors between worlds from swinging shut. The Ninth (the Caillte) is not a demon—it is a saint who forgot his own name. He cannot guide because he cannot be called. The Liturgy's highest calling is to remember him.

Saint Aodh'an the Herdsman (The Pale Shepherd)

Aodh'an was a herdsman who lost his flock in a blizzard. He searched for three days. On the third night, he saw a light moving through the snow—a lantern carried by a figure in gray. He followed the light to a cave. Inside, his flock was waiting, warm and unharmed. The figure in gray said: “You have found them. Now you will guide those who cannot find their own way.” Aodh'an became the first Tr'eada'. His lantern is the Shepherd's Lamp, carried by Gray Walkers. His feast day is the winter solstice.

Symbol: A lantern with a single gray flame.

Invocation: “Aodh'an, who found what was lost, guide this soul to the green hills. The snow is deep. The night is long. But your lamp burns.”

Saint Lasair'

ocht of the Bells (The Confessor Beneath the Bell)

Lasair'ocht was a nun who tended the dying in a plague village. She heard so many confessions that she began to carry the weight of the dead—their sins, their secrets, their unfinished business. One night, she rang the chapel bell at midnight. The bell cracked. The weight lifted from her shoulders and fell into the earth. A voice from the bell said: “You have carried enough. Now you will be the one who carries for others.” Lasair'ocht is the patron of confessors. Her bell is the Clog na Faoistine (Bell of Confession). Her feast day is the first of November—the day after Samhain, when the dead are closest.

Symbol: A cracked iron bell.

Invocation: “Lasair'ocht, who rang the bell at midnight, take this burden from my shoulders. Let the earth drink what I cannot swallow. Let the bell ring when I am empty.”

Saint Ciar'an of Balance (The Unbroken Way)

Ciar'an was a monk who spent seven years standing in a river, meditating, while the water flowed around him. He never moved. He never fell. When pilgrims asked how he remained still, he said: “I do not resist the water. I become it. The water flows through me. I am not still—I am the stillness between drops.” Ciar'an is the patron of Well-Walkers. His meditation is taught to all who fear death. His feast day is the spring equinox, when day and night are equal.

Symbol: A standing stone with a spiral carved into it.

Invocation: “Ciar'an, who stood in the river, steady my breath. The water flows around me, not through me. I am the stone. I am the still point.”

Saint F'

onntan of the Book (The Witness)

F'onntan was a scribe who copied every manuscript in his monastery. When the Vikings burned the library, he saved nothing—because he had memorised every word. He spent the rest of his life dictating what he had lost. He never forgave himself for not saving the books. But he never lied about what he remembered. F'onntan is the patron of Truth-Tellers. His ledger is not a book of judgment—it is a book of testimony. He records what happened, not what should have happened. His feast day is the autumn equinox.

Symbol: An open book with a single gray thread marking a page.

Invocation: “F'onntan, who remembered what was burned, witness this crossing. Write the name in your ledger. Do not judge. Do not forgive. Only record. The truth is enough.”

An Caillte (The Lost One — The Ninth)

An Caillte was once a saint like the others. But he forgot his own name. He wandered into the fog and never returned. Now he is the Dorcha—the Darkness. He is not evil. He is forgotten. The Gray Liturgy teaches that if someone can remember his true name, he will return and the Ninth threshold will become a door instead of a wound. But no one remembers. And every year, on the night of the dark moon, he knocks. The Gray Liturgy does not open the door. They wait. They listen. They hope.

Symbol: An empty circle. A threshold with no door.

Invocation: “An Caillte, whose name is lost, we do not call you. We cannot call you. But if you remember yourself, knock twice. We will open the door.”

Note: The Liturgy does not invoke An Caillte in the same way as the other saints. He is not called upon—he is listened for. Taboo-Breakers are those who have heard him knock and lived. They are the only ones permitted to approach the Ninth threshold.

Integration with Theona Generators

When using the Gray Liturgy in Theona, add the following sprinkles to the existing generators:

Spades (Places) — Add:

  • Cloch'an na gClog (Bell-Shrine) — A small stone hut on a misty headland. A single iron bell hangs inside, cracked and silent. Confessors ring it when a burden is transferred. The Viterran crown declared it a public nuisance. The bell rings anyway. The Abbess tried to melt it down. The bell rang in the forge. The forge went cold.
  • Tobar an Chaillte (Well of the Lost One) — A sacred well that no one admits exists. The water is black and still. Taboo-Breakers drink from it before their Well-Walk. The Viterran surveyors cannot find it on any map. The Abbess's clerics cannot find it at all. The Lady Beneath drinks from it.

Hearts (People) — Add:

  • Clogaire (Confessor) — A bell-ringer who carries the weight of the dead. Her hands are scarred from ringing. She never speaks of what she has heard. The Viterran sheriff tried to compel her testimony. She rang her bell. He withdrew the charge. The Abbess tried to buy her silence. She rang her bell. The Abbess's gold turned to ash.
  • Tr'eada' (Gray Walker) — A guide for the dying. He carries a lantern with a single gray flame. He sings the keening at deathbeds. The Viterran bishop declared his songs “unlicensed liturgy.” The songs continue. The Inquisitor declared them heretical. The Inquisitor died. The Tr'eada' sang him across.

Clubs (Complications) — Add:

  • The Unsung Bell (1 SB) — A confession is not enough. The Confessor cannot ring her bell. The weight must be carried until a witness volunteers.
  • The Ninth Knock (2 SB) — An Caillte knocks at the threshold. A door that was closed now rattles. The Gray Liturgy waits. The Green Host listens.
  • The Burdened Confessor (3 SB) — A Confessor collapses under the weight of unspoken sins. She cannot ring. She cannot speak. She can only wait for someone to carry her.

Diamonds (Rewards) — Add:

  • Bell-Ringer's Blessing — Once, you may ignore a Condition caused by guilt or despair. The Confessor rings her bell for you. The sound is flat, mournful, and final. The Viterran sheriff who received a blessing now sleeps through the night. The Abbess who received one now dreams only of bells.
  • Gray Thread — A gray thread tied around your wrist. Cut it to transfer a burden to a willing Confessor. The thread cannot be cut by the same hand that tied it. The Viterran governor who cut his own thread now carries his own weight. He is not sleeping. The Abbess who cut a thread for another now sleeps for both.

Regional Mood: Three Greens, No Ninth

Here, peace is a ritual, and every word sharpens the blade that seals it. Theona is claimed by Viterra but ruled by moots, well-keepers, and the old faith. The Viterran sheriffs count heads for the tax-roll; the Brehon judges measure truth by the witness of cattle and the memory of old words. The Viterran bishops raise hymns to the White Flame; the well-keepers leave milk and butter at the thorn crosses. The Everflame Inquisitors count sins in the silence between prayers. Every hedge is a boundary, every bridge a negotiation, every ninth step a door the Green Host might open. And in the mist-shrouded valleys, the Gray Liturgy keeps its candles lit and its bells waiting.

Linn dragon-prows cut through the fog for raiding; Ashaani slavers hunt the coves in stolen coracles; pirates from Zakov and the Vilikari shore trade stolen goods for kelp and salt. Sidhi sailors and Aelinnel factors run cargo up the tide-stairs, and Aelaerem hedge-wives barter red thread for hawthorn passes. To the west, across the narrow sound, the Viterran crown sharpens its taxes and its nooses. Through it all, the Ninth Taboo threads every handshake, every toast, every whispered prayer. To break it is to invite the Green Host—and the Host does not relent. To break Viterran law is to invite the sheriff's noose. To speak the silence is to invite the Everflame's brand. The Theona have learned to break neither—and to bend all three. The Gray Liturgy has learned to listen for the knock.

Starting Location: A Moot Hill under rain, where vows are carved into standing stone and blackthorn knives gleam beside the ogham pillar. A Bride-Peacemaker draws a blade between two bloodlines. “The ninth vow was never spoken,” she says. “But the Green Host remembers. Bring us the head of the slaver who burned the eastern strand, and the feud will end. Fail, and your name will join the uncounted. Or the sheriff will take you for vagrancy—the crown has declared our moots unlawful assemblies. Or the Abbess will call it heresy. Or, if you listen closely, the Confessor's bell will ring for you.”
